title: Lesson Planning Is Not the Basics: Why We're Training Teachers Backwards
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele argues that teacher training inverts the correct order of priority, treating full lesson-planning-from-scratch as the entry-level task for novice teachers when it should be the last skill they master. Quoting Dominic Salles's distinction between planning (the "Everest" of teaching) and the true basics (lesson starts, behaviour routines, transitions, scanning the room, vocal control, non-verbal intervention), Emanuele describes his own early career -- spending over 95% of his time planning lessons from scratch, going to bed past 2am, and struggling to master classroom basics with almost no time left for them. He frames this through cognitive load theory: novice teachers are simultaneously handling the intrinsic load of content and pedagogy, the extraneous load of designing slides and activities from nothing, and the classroom-management basics that require full attention on their own. His proposed fix is to give trainees and early-career teachers a high-quality, already-planned lesson sequence they can tweak, freeing their limited cognitive capacity to master cold call, mini whiteboards, and behaviour routines first.
points: Emanuele's central inversion argument, borrowed from Dominic Salles, is that lesson planning is treated as a "basic" novice task when it is actually the hardest skill in teaching, while the true basics (routines, transitions, vocal control, non-verbal intervention) are skipped over as assumed.

His personal account is stark and specific: over 95% of his early career time went to planning lessons from scratch, leaving almost no time to master classroom management, with regular nights working past 2am.

The cognitive load framing does real explanatory work: novice teachers face intrinsic load (content/pedagogy), extraneous load (designing materials from nothing), and classroom-management demands simultaneously, when Explicit Instruction's own principles say complex tasks should be scaffolded, not stacked.

His concrete fix -- give trainees a complete, evidence-informed lesson sequence (e.g. built on Rosenshine's Principles or I Do/We Do/You Do) that they can tweak rather than build from nothing -- is offered as reducing extraneous load specifically, not as removing teacher judgement.
quotes: Planning is not the basics. Planning is the be all and end all, the Alpha and Omega, the Everest of teaching.
The basics are lesson starts, behaviour routines, transitions, scanning the room, moving to each part of the room, vocal control, body language, gestures and non verbal intervention.
When I started teaching, more than 95% of my time was spent on one thing: planning lessons from scratch.

Think about the math for a moment. A full-time teacher needs to plan 4-5 one-hour lessons per day. If a truly good lesson planned from scratch takes, conservatively, one hour, you are signing up for 4-5 hours of planning every single day.

We are, as David Didau suggests, inviting stupidity in. We violate the core tenet of Explicit Instruction - that teaching should be scaffolded to reduce cognitive load - by handing the biggest, most complex task (full planning) to the least experienced person.
Let’s focus our newest colleagues on mastering the performance of teaching, not the production of resources. Give them the plan, and watch them become expert teachers faster.
